editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The evolute of a regular curve in the Euclidean planes is not only given by it's caustic, the envelope of it's normal lines, but also as the locus of singular points of it's parallel curves. In general, the evolute of a regular curve has singularities, since such points correspond to vertices of the regular curve and there are at least four vertices on simple closed curves. If we repeat an evolute, we cannot define the evolute at a singular point. In this paper, we define an evolute of a front and give properties of such an evolute by using a moving frame along a front and the curvature of the Legendre immersion. As applications, repeated evolutes are useful to recognize the shape of curves.

editorial_contributions.text: The authors study evolutes, caustics, and parallel curves of a smooth, regular curve \(\gamma\) in the pseudo-Euclidean plane (Minkowski plane). A point on \(\gamma\) is called ``space-like'', ``time-like, ``light-like'' if the tangent in this point is space-like, time-like, light-like, respectively. The behavior of caustics at light-like points of \(\gamma\) are discussed. For instance, \(\gamma\) and the caustic are tangent to each other in such a point and lie locally in distinct halfplanes determined by the common tangent. Another result is that the caustic of an oval curve \(\gamma\) lies in the exterior of \(\gamma\). A parallel curve to \(\gamma\) can be defined only at non-light-like points of \(\gamma\). The behavior of the Minkowski parallel curves at an ordinary vertex of \(\gamma\) is compared to the behavior of their Euclidean counterparts at such a point.

editorial_contributions.text:
This is a delightful and very useful introduction to geometry based on the interrelationship between a curve and its evolute, and a surface and its evolute surfaces. On the way, the author introduces all that is needed for the understanding of differential geometry and singularity classification, as well as applications of singularity theory. It is most highly recommended as an introduction to modern views of nonmetric differential geometry.


The first chapter deals with curves and their evolutes, introduces the singularities possible and impossible on evolutes, studies offset (parallel) curves, and ends with the four-vertices theorem. The next chapter teaches some technical details and methodical background material. Then comes a quick and elegant treatment of plane kinematics. A chapter on curves on the unit sphere leads to one on general space curves, their parallel curves and focal surfaces. The next two chapters are technical, one on quadratic and cubic forms, and one on normal forms (``probes'') of jets. A chapter on contact and contact equivalence leads to the study of surfaces and their lines of curvature, and then to the singularities, ridges and ribs, of the focal surfaces. The following chapters, containing the modern geometry, start out with Darboux's and other classifications of umbilics [the half-integer nature of the index at the umbilic being taken for granted], a detailed study of the parabolic line as introduction to Gauss curvature, and the study of the relations between the two sheets of the focal surface if some regularity condition on the surface is violated. [To appreciate the modern mathematics, this chapter should be compared to Chapter IX in \textit{L. Bianchi}, Lezioni di geometria differenziale, vol. I, parte II, Zanichelli (Bologna 1927)]. A final chapter applies the theory to several types of concrete surfaces. A few misprints are easily corrected. The name of the Russian master of singularities is Арнольд, not Ариопд!

title.title: Geometric differentiation for the intelligence of curves and surfaces

editorial_contributions.text:
This is not just another book on the local differential geometry of curves and surfaces: there are numerous textbooks on the topic but most modern textbooks give curves and surfaces only a very elementary treatment and leave concealed the richness of the theory, that becomes apparent when studying, for example, the classical textbooks of \textit{G. Darboux} [Leçons sur la théorie générale des surfaces et les applications géométriques du calcul infinitésimal. Vols. I--IV; Reprint, Chelsea, New York (1972; Zbl 0257.53001)], \textit{L. Bianchi} [Lezioni di geometria differenziale; Enrico Spoerri, Pisa (1923; JFM 49.0498.06)], or \textit{W. Blaschke} [Vorlesungen über Differentialgeometrie und geometrische Grundlagen von Einsteins Relativitätstheorie. I--III; Springer, Berlin (1930; JFM 56.0588.06), (1923; JFM 49.0499.01), and (1929; JFM 55.0422.01)]. The book under review is different. It touches upon a variety of interesting topics that are usually not to be found in textbooks, in particular, different kinds of singularities that naturally occur, for example, from certain constructions are discussed in detail. Also, the book leads the reader to current research results, by the author and his colleagues and by the Russian master V. I. Arnol'd of singularity theory and his school. This second edition of \textit{I. R. Porteous}' book extends the first edition (1994; Zbl 0806.53001) by the two chapters 17 and 18 on flexcords of surfaces and on curves and surfaces in the \(2\)- and \(3\)-sphere. 


Nevertheless the book certainly qualifies as a textbook, suitable for a course on curves and surfaces, as any material needed beyond a minimum background in analysis and linear algebra is discussed. Various ``real world'' examples are included that may motivate a student or make the material more accessible. 


The following details shall illustrate the above remarks: 


Chapter 1, ``Plane curves'', deals with (parametrized) curves in the Euclidean plane. The notion of curvature is introduced via contact with a (parametrized) circle. Regular and unit speed curves are only treated as special cases. Much attention is paid to the evolute (focal curve) -- evolvente relationship between curves, the parallel curves of a given curve are studied, and the various kinds of singularities that can occur in these constructions are discussed in detail. 


After some basic facts on (bi-) linear algebra, polynomials, projective, and inversive geometry have been collected in Chapter 2, the ideas developed in the first chapter are applied to ``Plane kinematics'' in Chapter 3: the inflection circle, ball point, cubic of stationary curvature, and the Burmester points of a rigid motion -- all being described in terms of special points of the orbits of the motion -- are discussed. The rolling of a curve on another curve, previously touched upon in the context of the evolventes of a curve, is taken up again. In the last section ``Caustics'' a connection to optics is drawn. 


The following Chapter~4, ``The derivative of a map'', provides the usual basics from multidimensional analysis that is needed in differential geometry. 


In Chapter~5, ``Curves on the unit sphere'', some of the ideas from the first chapters are carried over to the \(2\)-sphere: the geodesic curvature of a spherical curve is introduced, and some aspects of spherical kinematics are discussed, drawing a connection to geology (plate tectonics). 


Chapter~6, ``Space curves'', does indeed not only deal with space curves: before getting to the Frenet formula for a space curve and to the notion of parallel curves, the tangent developable of a space curve, the (space) evolute, and the focal surface (the tangent developable of the evolute) are discussed. Again, regularity questions and the occuring singularities are investigated. 


The following three chapters provide technical background: in Chapter~7, ``\(k\)-times linear forms'', some notions related to multilinear maps, quadratic, and cubic forms are introduced and the ``Use of complex numbers'' in this context, relevant to the study of surfaces, is explained; in Chapter~8, ``Probes'', a technique to investigate singularities of maps between vector spaces is introduced. The next short Chapter~9, ``Contact'', explains the notion of contact equivalence, which provides an application for the material from the previous chapter. 


Chapter~10, ``Surfaces in \(R^3\)'', starts with a comprehensive introduction that outlines what will be discussed in the following chapters, in particular, concerning the relation between a surface and its focal surface (evolute). After this introduction the usual material is covered: the first and second fundamental forms and the principal curvatures are discussed. Considering the corresponding centres of curvature one is led to the evolute of a surface, and first relations between the surface and its focal surface are discussed; in particular it is shown that the curvature lines of the surface yield geodesics of the evolute where it is regular. 


Chapter~11, ``Ridges and Ribs'', then discusses the various types of singularities that the focal surface of a regular surface can have. An important idea is to consider the ``normal focal surface'' as a surface in the tangent bundle of Euclidean \(3\)-space. Chapter~12, ``Umbilics'', continues the investigation of isolated umbilics begun in the preceding chapter. In particular the shape of the principal curvature lines around an umbilic is discussed, and ways to classify umbilics are presented. Here the discussions are more colloquial, a short section on the index of an umbilic collects some facts without proofs -- however, many references to classical and modern literature are given where the reader may find more detailed information. Remarks on parallel surfaces and on the effect of deformation of a surface on umbilics conclude the chapter. 


Chapter~13, ``The parabolic line'', is concerned with the locus of parabolic points (points of Gaussian curvature \(0\)) of a surface. It starts with a proof of Gauss' theorema egregium, and then turns to a description of the singularities of the Gauss map at parabolic points. Koenderink's theorems on the relation between the Gaussian curvature of a surface and its contour under a parallel or central projection, respectively, are presented and the consequences for parabolic points are investigated -- thus establishing a connection to shape recognition. Finally the subparabolic lines of a regular surface are studied: these are the lines that correspond to parabolic lines on the focal surface; in particular, their behaviour at umbilics is related to that of the curvature lines of the surface. 


The reconstruction of a surface from (one sheet of) its evolute is the theme of Chapter~14, ``Involutes of geodesic foliations'': the starting point here is the earlier observation that the curvature lines of a surface yield geodesics on the focal surface; the reconstruction then proceeds similar to the case of planar curves. However, assuming the evolute to be regular its involute may develop certain types of singularities that are discussed in detail. Finally, Coxeter groups are brought into play and it is outlined how they give rise to singularities of curves or surfaces -- at this point the labeling of singularities in the book under review is explained. 


Chapter~15, ``The circles of a surface'', deals with osculating circles of a surface. At the basis of the discussions is Meusnier's classical theorem. As a refinement of this theorem the existence of higher order osculating circles in a given direction is related to various types of points of the surface discussed earlier throughout the book, in particular, to umbilics. In case the Meusnier sphere becomes the tangent plane of the surface, the geometry of its intersection curve with the surface is examined. Using, as explained at the end of Chapter~13, an inversion to flatten the Meusnier sphere these investigations carry over to the Meusnier sphere. 


In Chapter~16, ``Examples of surfaces'', the theory presented in the preceding chapters is exemplified: among the discussed surfaces are the general ellipsoid, bumpy spheres that emanate from perturbing the equation of the unit sphere by a (small) third order term, and the minimal monkey saddle. 


Chapter~17, ``Flexcords of surfaces'', is the first of two new chapters: it takes up the discussion of subparabolic lines (now called flexcords) from Chapter~13 and presents recent developments on the subject. In particular, flexcord points of implicitly given surfaces are characterized; and the ``birth'' or ``death'' of umbilics, touched upon earlier in Chapter~12, is discussed in more detail -- bumpy spheres provide an interesting example. 


The second new Chapter~18, ``Duality'', deals with Arnol'd's notions of the dual and the derivative curve of an (oriented) curve in the \(2\)-sphere, thus complementing material from Chapter~5, and with generalizations of these notions to surfaces and curves in the \(3\)-sphere. Singularities that occur from these constructions are examined, and implications for the respective evolutes are discussed. 


In each chapter a set of exercises is formulated. 


The reviewer found this an interesting and inspiring book, a slight drawback only being the fact that definitions are incorporated into the text which makes it harder to locate them -- as a consequence the reviewer failed in a first attempt to start reading the book in the middle. Many instructive illustrations can help the reader to understand the discussed notions and facts, and many interesting historical remarks and references are given throughout the text.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: On fine scales, caustics produced with white light show vividly colored diffraction fringes. For caustics described by the elementary catastrophes of singularity theory, the colors are characteristic of the type of singularity. We study the diffraction colors of the fold and cusp catastrophes. The colors can be simulated computationally as the superposition of monochromatic patterns for different wavelengths. Far from the caustic, where the luminosity contrast is negligible, the fringe colors persist; an asymptotic theory explains why. Experiments with caustics produced by refraction through irregular bathroom-window glass show good agreement with theory. Colored fringes near the cusp reveal fine lines that are not present in any of the monochromatic components; these lines are explained in terms of partial decoherence between rays with widely differing path differences.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper studies circular evolutes and involutes of framed curves in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). It starts with a brief review of the theory of framed curves and surfaces. Given an interval \(I\) of \(\mathbb{R}\), a framed curve is a smooth map 
\[
(\gamma,\nu_1,\nu_2):I\to\mathbb{R}^3\times\Delta,
\]
where \(\Delta=\{( x, y)\in S^2\times S^2: x\cdot y=0\}\), such that \(\dot\gamma(t)\) is orthogonal to both \(\nu_1(t)\) and \(\nu_2(t)\). Writing \(\mu=\nu_1\times\nu_2\), one obtains a moving orthonormal frame \((\nu_1,\nu_2,\mu)\) satisfying a Frenet-type system with four curvature functions \((\ell,m,n,\alpha)\). This framework allows the treatment of curves with singular points, for which the classical Frenet frame is not available. A Bishop direction is a unit normal vector field obtained by rotating \((\nu_1,\nu_2)\) through an angle \(\theta\) satisfying \(\theta'=-\ell\). %A Bishop frame along \(\gamma\) is constructed by two orthogonal Bishop directions and their cross product.

The first part of the paper introduces \(v\)-parallel curves and \(v\)-normal surfaces of framed curves. A \(v\)-parallel curve of a framed curve \(\gamma\) with a rotated frame \(\{v,w,\mu\}\) is the space curve \(P_{\gamma}[v]\) defined by 
\[
P_{\gamma}[v](t)=\gamma(t)+\lambda\, v(t)
\] 
for a fixed \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\). A characterization of \(P_{\gamma}[v]\) being a framed curve in terms of the existence of a smooth function is given. Similarly, \(v\)-normal surfaces of framed curves are defined as ruled surfaces with respect to \(v\) and a characterization is given. The singularities of these normal surfaces are studied. Then, the authors consider normal surfaces of framed curves with respect to certain Bishop directions and the corresponding singularity criteria for a cuspidal edge, a swallowtail, and a cuspidal cross cap are given.

In the second part of the paper, circular evolutes and involutes of framed curves are defined under appropriate assumptions. Some properties are studied and it is shown that, under appropriate assumptions, taking the circular evolute and taking the involute are shown to be inverse operations, similar to the relation between evolutes and involutes of fronts in the Euclidean plane. The paper also studies the relations between the singularities of normal surfaces, circular evolutes and involutes of framed curves, and includes several illustrative examples.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1582.58002].

title.title: Circular evolutes and involutes of framed curves in the 3-dimensional Euclidean space

editorial_contributions.text:
The theory of singularities of manifolds is usually studied from an algebraic point of view rather than from a differential one. The authors of the book under review have covered this lack writing a text, which is comprehensible for undergraduate students having a certain background on classical theories of differentiable curves and surfaces. In fact, the basic notions of these theories are summarized obtaining a self-contained text. As the authors point out several times, deeper results can be understood by readers knowing the theory of smooth manifolds. The book is carefully written, beginning with basic notions and detailed examples, and rising elaborated results where the authors are reputed experts. Examples and exercises of the book are very useful to understand different notions.

A `leitmotiv' of the book is that of singularities arising in wave fronts, that we can, roughly speaking, define as parallel curves or surfaces to a given one. The book is divided in 10 chapters and 8 appendices. The first chapter is devoted to the study of singularities of planar curves and all of the rest to the study of singularities in surfaces (the last one is devoted to manifolds). The first two chapters provide the reader with a robust understanding of singularities of planar curves and surfaces: different classes of cusps of planar curves, and cuspidal edges, swallowtails, cross caps and cuspidal cross caps of surfaces. In Chapters 3 and 4 one finds the proofs of the criteria for the singularities introduced before, and Gauss-Bonnet type formulas for surfaces with singularities. There is no easy generalization of the classical Gauss-Bonnet formula to this kind of surfaces. Here two formulas are presented, after carefully recalling the classical one, and some other results of Gauss-Bonnet formulas are obtained in the following chapters.

The last six chapters use manifolds theory, although the results are about surfaces. For instance, Gauss-Bonnet theorem remains for 2-dimensional Riemannian manifolds, and such surfaces with singularities are also considered. In Chapter 5 curvature on singular points is studied, whilst in Chapter 6 the authors prove both kind of formulas of Gauss-Bonnet type, both in the local and in the global cases. Chapter 7 is devoted to analyzing flat surfaces of \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\), beginning with singularities of caustic (focal) surfaces. In Chapter 8 one can find a proof of the criterion of swallowtails singularities. The relation between wave fronts and coherent tangent bundles is shown in Chapter 9. The last chapter has a different nature, because the authors consider wave fronts on manifolds being able to show them from the viewpoint of contact geometry.

The book is very well written. The authors refer to their own books on classical differential geometry of curves and surfaces as background, but the book is written in a self-contained style allowing any reader with basic knowledge to understand it. Thus, the book provides a very nice introduction to singularities of curves and surfaces. Moreover, researches in the area will enjoy having this clear exposition of the theory that also includes sophisticated notions.

title.title: Differential geometry of curves and surfaces with singularities. Translated from the Japanese by Wayne Rossman

editorial_contributions.text:
This is a nice introductory book to geometry written in French. It is addressed to students of mathematics and physics as well as engineers. The material of the book is developed smoothly and rigorously. The proofs are solid and clear. Without doubt, the book can help the reader to develop intuition in geometry and sharpen geometric way of thinking. There are interesting applications of the theory and many exercises of various difficulty which are very well related to the text. Finally the book can be studied easily as the major part of it is self-contained and prerequisites are kept down to first semester course in linear algebra and analysis.

In the following basic topics of the book are presented.

The book is divided into three parts. The first part contains two chapters. The first chapter contains a new axiomatic formulation of geometry based on seven axioms and follows the spirit of Birkhoff. It uses a set theoretic language and assumes the existence of the field of real numbers. The 3-space is a set and its subsets are the geometric figures. The fundamental axiom associates to each pair of \(A,\) \(B\) in 3-space a real number which is the distance of these points. Afterwards the notions of vector and vector space are defined. In the second chapter the coordinates of a point are defined, using the notion of affine frame. As a consequence the concept of analytic geometry is introduced. In the following the homogeneous and barycentric coordinates of a point are defined. As a nice application of barycentric coordinates the classical theorems of Menelaus, Ceva and Pappus are proven. The chapter finishes with an interesting application in the theory of colors.

The second part contains three chapters. In the chapter three and four basic products between vectors are defined namely, the scalar, exterior, vectorial and mixed product. The area of plane regions is defined and by means of it, the concept of angle between vectors is defined. Nice applications to the geometry of triangles as well as to the geometry of lines and planes are given. In the fifth chapter the affine transformations and the isometries of the plane and of 3-space are defined. The main Theorem (Chasles theorem) of this chapter is the classification of isometries as well as a decomposition theorem of the affine transformations. The chapter finishes with the notion of group and with basic examples of groups.

The third part of the book is dedicated to differential geometry. It is divided in two chapters, chapter six and chapter seven. In chapter six the fundamental notions and facts concerning the curves in the plane and in 3-space are presented. A characterization of curves of constant slope is given and it is proven that a regular curve in the space is determined, under isometry, from its curvature and torsion. The author studies extensively plane curves and it is proven that each continuous function arises as curvature of a plane curve of class \(C^2\). The concept of evolute and involute of a curve is defined and the theorem of Huygens which relates the evolute with the involute is proven. The most important examples of plane curves are given and the envelope of a family of curves is studied.

The seventh chapter presents an introduction to the theory of surfaces in 3-space where the most important aspects of this theory are explained. There are some explicit calculations here, but the author succeeds to clearly demonstrate all the geometric ideas of the theory. The normal curvature as well as, the mean curvature and the Gauss curvature is defined. The concept of uniformly extendable surface is explained and by means of it, minimal surfaces are defined. In the following the second fundamental form and the shape operator \(L\) are explained. It is proven that the mean curvature and the Gauss curvature are equal to minus the half of the trace of \(L\) and to the determinant of \(L\), respectively. The Christoffel symbols are defined and it is proven that they can be expressed algebraically by means of the first fundamental form and its derivatives. Finally it is proven that the Gauss curvature can be expressed as a function of the first fundamental form and of the Christoffel symbols. From this, it is deduced immediately the Theorema egregium of Gauss that asserts that the Gauss curvature is an intrinsic notion depending only of the surface and not of the position of the surface in the 3-space.

In conclusion, the book is highly recommended for an introduction to elementary geometry and to differential geometry of curves and surfaces.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper studies singularities of parallel curves and evolutes of frontal curves in the Euclidean plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and some associated lifted surfaces in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to parallel curves whose initial curve has singularities. For a regular planar curve, singular points of parallel curves are known to be located on the evolute, and the relationship between the types of singularities for parallel and evolutes is known. This paper mainly focuses on frontal curves that admit a \(5/2\)-cusp or a \(5/3\)-cusp as isolated singular points. After the author introduces some notions on frontal curves in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and frontal surfaces in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the behavior of curvature functions of frontal curves arising from a moving frame at a singular point is studied. Parallels of frontal curves are considered and their singularities are characterized by singularities of the initial frontal curve and geometric invariants.

From another point of view, the evolute of a regular planar curve is the singular locus of the normal congruence (or normal ruling map) of the curve. In this paper, normal congruences of frontal curves are considered. In contrast to the regular case, the singular loci of normal congruences of frontal curves consist of the evolute and a line that is normal to the initial curve at the singular point. The singularity types are also studied.

Finally, the last part of the paper treats certain lifted surfaces associated to parallels of planar frontal curves that, naturally, are seen to be frontal surfaces in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) that are developable surfaces. Moreover, the lifted surface is given as a tangent developable surface of a certain spatial curve related to the evolute of the initial frontal curve. A condition that the lifted surface has a Scherbak singularity is also given. Focal surfaces of lifted surfaces are considered as well and some results on their singularities and involving the mean curvature are given.
